comment: Bb7 puts the bishop where a rook on d7 will hit it, and leaves d7 open for exactly that. 16...Bd7 (+2.7 instead of +3.3) guards c6 and plugs the d-file, so White's rooks have no entry square. Black is worse either way (king in the centre, c6 and a6 weak, rook h8 asleep), but Bd7 keeps the rooks out.

variations.comment: +2.7: White still wins c6, but the order is Rhd1 first, then Bf3. Worth remembering for the next move.

comment: The plan was Bf3 to hit c6, then double on the 7th ("l'idée ce serait de doubler sur la septième rangée"). The order is wrong. Bf3 leaves the d6 rook without a defender, and 17...Ke7! hits it with tempo: now Bxc6 fails to ...Kxd6, the king covers d7 so the 7th rank is shut, and after the forced Rhd1 Black plays ...Rad8 and trades all four rooks into a same-coloured bishop ending worth only +0.7. 17.Rhd1 first (+3.4) protects d6, and then ...Ke7 is met by Rd7+ winning the b7 bishop. Once the rooks are on the d-file, Bf3 and Bxc6 come later with no counterplay. Rule: when an advanced rook is undefended, defend it before starting the attack.

comment: 17...Rd8 attacks the d6 rook but ignores c6, which Bf3 and Rd6 hit twice while only the b7 bishop defends it. 18.Bxc6+ takes the pawn with check. After ...Bxc6 Rxc6 the rook has left d6, so ...Rd8 has nothing to hit. 17...Ke7! (+0.7) was the move: it attacks d6 from a square where Bxc6 is no longer check (...Kxd6 wins a rook for bishop and pawn), then ...Rad8 trades everything down. After 19.Rxc6 White is a pawn up with a 3-v-1 queenside majority (a, b and c against Black's a-pawn), and the c6 rook hits a6 and e6 while the h8 rook and e8 king are still undeveloped: +3.6.
